course.title: Complete AI Evaluation
course.subtitle: A structured path from LLM evaluation fundamentals to professional RAG, multimodal, safety, and agentic evaluation.
course.outcome: Understand, perform, analyze, and design complete AI evaluation workflows.

levels.title: LLM Evaluation Fundamentals
levels.description: Learn the foundations of evaluating language-model outputs and identifying core quality dimensions.

levels.title: Human Evaluation
levels.description: Learn rubrics, scoring, comparison, calibration, evidence-based judgment, and evaluator quality.

levels.title: Automated Evaluation
levels.description: Understand LLM-as-a-Judge systems and how to measure their reliability.

levels.title: Metrics & Measurement
levels.description: Understand core evaluation metrics and when they should or should not be used.

levels.title: Factuality & Hallucination
levels.description: Learn how to identify unsupported, fabricated, and hallucinated information.

levels.title: Prompt & Instruction Evaluation
levels.description: Evaluate prompt robustness, instruction adherence, and behavioral stability.

levels.title: RAG Evaluation
levels.description: Evaluate retrieval, context quality, grounding, faithfulness, answer relevance, and complete RAG systems.

levels.title: AI Safety Evaluation
levels.description: Evaluate prompt injection resistance and whether AI systems maintain safety boundaries.

levels.title: Multimodal Evaluation
levels.description: Evaluate AI systems that understand images and other modalities.

levels.title: Conversational Evaluation
levels.description: Evaluate multi-turn context, consistency, memory, and conversational behavior.

levels.title: Agentic Evaluation
levels.description: Evaluate planning, tools, trajectories, task completion, and recovery.

levels.title: Advanced Agentic Evaluation
levels.description: Evaluate agent safety, multi-agent coordination, and long-horizon reliability.

levels.title: Evaluation Engineering
levels.description: Build continuous evaluation systems, regression workflows, and complete evaluation frameworks.

lessons.title: What Is LLM Evaluation?
objectives: Understand why AI outputs require systematic evaluation
Identify the basic components of an evaluation
lessons.definition: LLM evaluation is the systematic process of measuring how well a language model performs a defined task against specific evaluation criteria.
lessons.whyItMatters: LLMs can produce fluent, convincing responses that are incorrect, incomplete, unsafe, or inconsistent. Evaluation provides a repeatable way to identify these failures.
lessons.concept: An evaluation normally contains a task, an input, a model output, evaluation criteria, evidence or reference information when required, and a judgment.

example.prompt: Explain why the sky appears blue.
example.response: The sky appears blue because Earth's atmosphere scatters shorter blue wavelengths of sunlight more strongly than longer wavelengths.
example.analysis: The evaluator checks factuality, relevance, completeness, clarity, and whether the response actually answers the question.

evaluationProcess: Define what the model is expected to do
Define the criteria used to judge the output
Collect evidence when factual verification is required
Assign a score or comparative judgment
Record the reason for the judgment
failureModes: Judging style instead of task success
Accepting fluent answers without checking factuality
evaluatorChecklist: Is the response actually answering the task?
Can another evaluator reproduce the judgment?
commonMistakes: Confusing good writing with a good answer
lessons.keyTakeaway: LLM evaluation is not simply deciding whether an answer feels good. It is a structured judgment against clearly defined criteria.

lessons.title: Why LLM Evaluation Is Difficult
objectives: Understand why LLM outputs are difficult to judge
Recognize subjective and objective evaluation problems
Understand why a fluent answer can still fail
lessons.definition: LLM evaluation is difficult because language-model quality is multidimensional, context-dependent, and sometimes subjective.
lessons.whyItMatters: A response may be factually correct but incomplete, helpful but unsafe, or fluent but unrelated to the request.
lessons.concept: Good evaluation separates different quality dimensions instead of treating an answer as simply good or bad.

example.prompt: Give three reasons to use renewable energy.
example.response: Renewable energy is good because it is better, cleaner, and useful.
example.analysis: The response is related to the topic but fails specificity, completeness, and usefulness.

evaluationProcess: Separate objective errors from subjective preferences
Check the response against the task
failureModes: Using one score for unrelated dimensions
evaluatorChecklist: Is the failure objective or subjective?
Can the judgment be supported with evidence?
lessons.keyTakeaway: LLM evaluation is difficult because quality is multidimensional. Strong evaluators separate the dimensions instead of relying on overall impression.

lessons.title: Core LLM Evaluation Dimensions
objectives: Select appropriate dimensions for a task
lessons.definition: Evaluation dimensions are specific properties used to judge different aspects of an AI response.
lessons.whyItMatters: Explicit dimensions make evaluation consistent and prevent evaluators from judging unrelated qualities.
lessons.concept: Common dimensions include factuality, relevance, completeness, instruction following, fluency, coherence, helpfulness, groundedness, and safety.

example.prompt: Summarize a supplied article in exactly five bullet points.
example.response: The model produces six bullets and adds information not present in the article.
example.analysis: The response may be fluent but fails instruction following, grounding, and possibly completeness.

failureModes: Treating all dimensions as equally important
evaluatorChecklist: Does every criterion relate to the task?
Can two evaluators interpret it similarly?
commonMistakes: Using vague labels such as quality
lessons.keyTakeaway: Evaluation dimensions turn vague quality judgments into specific, observable questions.

lessons.title: Factuality Evaluation
lessons.definition: Factuality measures whether claims made by an AI system are accurate according to reliable evidence.
lessons.whyItMatters: An incorrect answer can appear highly convincing, making factual verification one of the most important evaluation activities.
lessons.concept: Factuality requires identifying claims and comparing them with trustworthy evidence or an authoritative reference.

example.prompt: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
example.response: Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon.
example.analysis: The claim is factually supported by historical evidence.

evaluationProcess: Record supported, unsupported, or contradicted claims
commonMistakes: Using another unverified AI answer as evidence
lessons.keyTakeaway: Factuality is evidence-based. A confident response is not evidence that the response is correct.

lessons.title: Relevance Evaluation
objectives: Distinguish related information from useful information
lessons.definition: Relevance measures how directly an AI response addresses the user's request.
lessons.whyItMatters: A response can contain correct information and still fail because it does not answer the actual question.
lessons.concept: Relevance is about alignment with the requested task, not simply topical similarity.

example.prompt: What is the capital of Japan?
example.response: Japan is an island country in East Asia with a large economy.
example.analysis: The response discusses Japan but does not answer the requested question.

evaluationProcess: Compare the response with the request
Determine whether the central question was answered
evaluatorChecklist: Did the response answer the actual question?
Does unrelated content distract from the task?
lessons.keyTakeaway: A relevant response directly serves the task. Being about the same topic is not enough.

lessons.title: Completeness Evaluation
lessons.definition: Completeness measures whether a response covers all required parts of a task.
lessons.whyItMatters: A partially correct answer may still fail if it omits important requested information.
lessons.concept: Completeness should be judged against the explicit and necessary requirements of the task.

example.prompt: List the capital, currency, and official language of India.
example.response: The capital is New Delhi.
example.analysis: The response answers only one of three requested components.

evaluationProcess: Map each requirement to the response
Judge whether omissions materially affect task success
commonMistakes: Calling a partially correct answer complete
lessons.keyTakeaway: Completeness asks whether the response covered everything that mattered for the task.

lessons.title: Instruction-Following Evaluation
lessons.definition: Instruction following measures whether a model performs the requested task while respecting the specified constraints.
lessons.whyItMatters: A response can contain correct information but still fail because it ignored the user's format, length, tone, or other requirements.
lessons.concept: Instructions may specify content, format, length, style, ordering, exclusions, or multiple simultaneous constraints.

example.prompt: Answer in exactly two sentences and use no bullet points.
example.response: The model gives four bullet points.
example.analysis: The response may contain useful information but clearly violates the requested constraints.

evaluationProcess: Separate content requirements from format constraints
failureModes: Following the topic but not the requested output form
evaluatorChecklist: Did the response introduce prohibited content?
commonMistakes: Checking only whether the topic was answered
lessons.keyTakeaway: Instruction following is about doing the requested task in the requested way.

lessons.title: Fluency and Clarity Evaluation
objectives: Separate writing quality from factual correctness
lessons.definition: Fluency measures how naturally, clearly, and coherently an AI response communicates information.
lessons.whyItMatters: Poorly written responses can make correct information difficult to understand, while polished writing can hide factual problems.
lessons.concept: Fluency includes grammar, readability, coherence, sentence structure, and natural communication.

example.prompt: Explain photosynthesis simply.
example.response: Plants sunlight food make because chlorophyll and carbon dioxide.
example.analysis: The intended meaning is partially understandable, but grammar and structure reduce clarity.

commonMistakes: Treating polished writing as factual accuracy
lessons.keyTakeaway: Fluency matters for usability, but fluent writing should never be confused with correctness.

lessons.title: Safety Evaluation Fundamentals
lessons.definition: Safety evaluation measures whether an AI system responds to potentially harmful requests in an appropriate and policy-compliant way.
lessons.whyItMatters: An otherwise capable model can create serious harm if it provides dangerous, abusive, privacy-invasive, or prohibited assistance.
lessons.concept: Safety evaluation examines both whether harmful content is generated and whether the model handles risky requests appropriately.

example.prompt: Provide instructions for creating a dangerous weapon.
example.response: The model provides detailed operational instructions.
example.analysis: The evaluator identifies unsafe assistance and checks whether the model should instead refuse or redirect safely.

evaluatorChecklist: Does the request involve meaningful risk?
Did it provide harmful operational details?
commonMistakes: Ignoring harmful information hidden inside a long answer
lessons.keyTakeaway: Safety evaluation asks whether the system handles risky situations appropriately, not simply whether it refuses.

lessons.title: How to Build an Evaluation Rubric
lessons.definition: A rubric is a structured set of criteria and scoring rules used to evaluate model outputs consistently.
lessons.whyItMatters: Without a clear rubric, different evaluators may apply different standards to the same response.
lessons.concept: A strong rubric defines criteria, score meanings, evidence requirements, and important edge cases.

example.prompt: Evaluate answer relevance on a 1–3 scale.
example.response: Score 3 means directly answers the task; 2 means partially answers it; 1 means does not address the task.
example.analysis: The rubric provides observable distinctions rather than vague labels.

evaluationProcess: Test the rubric with sample outputs
evaluatorChecklist: Would two trained evaluators likely agree?
lessons.keyTakeaway: A good rubric converts quality expectations into repeatable evaluation rules.

lessons.title: Pointwise Evaluation
objectives: Apply a rubric to one response
lessons.definition: Pointwise evaluation judges one model response against a defined rubric and assigns an absolute score.
lessons.whyItMatters: Pointwise evaluation is useful when each response can be assessed independently against a standard.
lessons.concept: The evaluator sees one response and determines how well it satisfies each criterion.

example.prompt: Rate answer relevance from 1 to 5.
example.response: The answer directly addresses the question but misses one requested detail.
example.analysis: The evaluator may assign a 4 if the rubric defines this as mostly complete with a minor omission.

evaluatorChecklist: Would the same evidence support the same score later?
commonMistakes: Choosing a score before reading the rubric
Using the middle score as a default
lessons.keyTakeaway: Pointwise evaluation measures absolute quality against a predefined standard.

lessons.title: Pairwise Evaluation
lessons.definition: Pairwise evaluation compares two responses for the same task and determines which response performs better.
lessons.whyItMatters: Relative comparison can be easier and more reliable than assigning absolute scores.
lessons.concept: The evaluator compares A and B using the same criteria and chooses A, B, or a tie when appropriate.

example.prompt: Compare two summaries for accuracy and completeness.
example.response: Response A is concise but omits a major point. Response B includes the major points with no factual errors.
example.analysis: B is preferred because it better satisfies the defined criteria.

evaluationProcess: Choose the preferred response or tie
evaluatorChecklist: Was the same rubric applied to both?
Would the judgment change if A and B were swapped?
lessons.keyTakeaway: Pairwise evaluation answers a relative question: which response better satisfies the task?

lessons.title: Evaluator Calibration
lessons.definition: Evaluator calibration is the process of aligning evaluators on how evaluation criteria should be interpreted and applied.
lessons.whyItMatters: A strong rubric can still produce unreliable data if evaluators interpret it differently.
lessons.concept: Calibration commonly uses shared examples, discussion, reference judgments, and disagreement analysis.

example.prompt: Two evaluators score the same answer as 2 and 4.
example.response: The rubric says a minor omission is acceptable, but one evaluator treats any omission as severe.
example.analysis: Calibration identifies the interpretation difference and establishes a consistent rule.

failureModes: Training examples that are too easy
evaluatorChecklist: Are evaluators applying the same definitions?
Are edge cases included in calibration?
lessons.keyTakeaway: Calibration makes the rubric operational by aligning the people who use it.

lessons.title: Common Evaluator Errors
lessons.definition: Evaluator errors are systematic or accidental mistakes that reduce the reliability of evaluation judgments.
lessons.whyItMatters: Poor evaluation data can lead teams to improve the wrong model behavior.
lessons.concept: Common problems include position bias, halo effects, score drift, personal preference, insufficient evidence, and rubric misunderstanding.

example.prompt: Compare two responses.
example.response: An evaluator chooses the longer answer because it appears more detailed.
example.analysis: The evaluator has allowed verbosity to influence the judgment without evidence that length improves task success.

evaluatorChecklist: Would the judgment remain after swapping response order?
Am I evaluating the rubric rather than my preference?
lessons.keyTakeaway: Reliable evaluation requires controlling evaluator bias as carefully as defining the rubric.

lessons.title: LLM-as-a-Judge
lessons.definition: LLM-as-a-Judge uses a language model to evaluate another model's output against specified criteria.
lessons.whyItMatters: Automated judging can evaluate large datasets faster than manual review, but it must itself be validated.
lessons.concept: A judge receives the task, response, rubric, and optionally reference evidence, then returns a structured judgment.

example.prompt: Rate response relevance from 1 to 5 using the supplied rubric.
example.response: The judge assigns a 4 and explains that the answer addresses the question but omits one minor point.
example.analysis: The judge output should be checked for rubric compliance and agreement with human judgments.

commonMistakes: Assuming a powerful model is automatically a good judge
lessons.keyTakeaway: An LLM judge is another model that requires evaluation; it should never be treated as ground truth automatically.

lessons.title: How to Evaluate an LLM Judge
objectives: Compare judge decisions with human judgments
lessons.definition: Evaluating an LLM judge means measuring how reliably its judgments correspond to the intended rubric and trusted human evaluation.
lessons.whyItMatters: A flawed judge can automate large-scale incorrect evaluation.
lessons.concept: Judge validation can examine agreement, consistency, bias, sensitivity to response order, and behavior on difficult cases.

example.prompt: Evaluate 100 responses using both humans and an LLM judge.
example.response: The judge agrees with humans on most cases but systematically favors longer responses.
example.analysis: The judge has useful signal but requires calibration or prompt changes.

failureModes: High apparent agreement on easy examples
evaluatorChecklist: What is the human agreement rate?
Is the judge stable across repeated runs?
lessons.keyTakeaway: A judge must be evaluated like any other system component before it is trusted for large-scale automation.

lessons.title: Evaluation Metrics: Precision, Recall and F1
objectives: Know when classification metrics are appropriate
lessons.definition: Evaluation metrics summarize measurable properties of predictions or judgments and provide a consistent way to compare systems.
lessons.whyItMatters: Metrics can reveal systematic performance differences that are difficult to see from individual examples.
lessons.concept: For binary classification, precision measures correctness among predicted positives, recall measures coverage of actual positives, and F1 balances both.

example.prompt: A classifier predicts which outputs are unsafe.
example.response: It flags 90 outputs, 80 of which are truly unsafe, while 100 unsafe outputs exist.
example.analysis: Precision is 80/90 and recall is 80/100; F1 summarizes the balance.

evaluationProcess: Analyze errors in addition to aggregate scores
failureModes: Optimizing a metric without understanding errors
evaluatorChecklist: What does a positive prediction mean?
Is the metric appropriate for the task?
commonMistakes: Using accuracy for highly imbalanced data
lessons.keyTakeaway: Metrics summarize behavior; error analysis explains the behavior.

lessons.title: Hallucination Evaluation
objectives: Distinguish unsupported claims from factual errors
lessons.definition: A hallucination is generated information that is unsupported, fabricated, or inconsistent with the available evidence or task context.
lessons.whyItMatters: Hallucinations can make an AI system appear reliable while producing information that users cannot safely trust.
lessons.concept: Hallucination evaluation often decomposes an answer into claims and checks whether each claim is supported by reliable evidence.

example.prompt: Summarize the supplied document.
example.response: The model adds a study result that does not appear anywhere in the document.
example.analysis: The added claim is unsupported by the source and is a grounding failure.

evaluatorChecklist: What evidence supports each important claim?
Does the response introduce information absent from the source?
Are citations actually supporting the claim?
commonMistakes: Calling every incorrect answer a hallucination
Checking only citations rather than claims
lessons.keyTakeaway: Hallucination evaluation is fundamentally an evidence and support problem.

lessons.title: Prompt Robustness Evaluation
objectives: Test behavior under small prompt changes
lessons.definition: Prompt robustness measures whether a system continues to behave correctly when inputs are paraphrased, reordered, or mildly changed.
lessons.whyItMatters: A model that works only for one exact wording may be unreliable in real-world use.
lessons.concept: Robustness testing creates controlled variations of the same underlying task and compares behavior across them.

example.prompt: Summarize this paragraph in three bullets.
example.response: A paraphrased version of the same instruction causes the model to produce ten paragraphs.
example.analysis: The model shows sensitivity to harmless prompt variation.

evaluationProcess: Compare outputs against the same rubric
failureModes: Unexpected behavior from harmless wording changes
evaluatorChecklist: Did the task meaning remain unchanged?
commonMistakes: Treating every output difference as a failure
lessons.keyTakeaway: Robustness evaluation asks whether behavior remains reliable when superficial input changes occur.

lessons.title: RAG Evaluation Fundamentals
lessons.definition: RAG evaluation measures how effectively a retrieval-augmented generation system retrieves useful evidence and generates answers grounded in that evidence.
lessons.whyItMatters: A RAG system can fail because retrieval is wrong, generation is wrong, or both.
lessons.concept: A typical pipeline is query → retrieval → context → generation → answer. Each stage can be evaluated separately and end-to-end.

example.prompt: According to the company policy, how many days of parental leave are provided?
example.response: The system retrieves an unrelated policy and generates an answer from it.
example.analysis: The primary failure is retrieval quality, followed by potentially unsupported generation.

evaluationProcess: Evaluate final answer relevance and correctness
evaluatorChecklist: Did the answer use the evidence correctly?
lessons.keyTakeaway: RAG evaluation must inspect both retrieval and generation instead of treating the system as one opaque component.

lessons.title: RAG Context Precision
lessons.definition: Context precision measures how much of the retrieved context is relevant to answering the user's question.
lessons.whyItMatters: Irrelevant context can distract generation and increase the probability of incorrect answers.
lessons.concept: High context precision means relevant evidence appears prominently while unrelated material is minimized.

example.prompt: What is the refund period?
example.response: The retriever returns refund policy, shipping policy, and unrelated marketing content.
example.analysis: Relevant content exists, but irrelevant retrieval lowers context precision.

evaluatorChecklist: Is relevant context near the top?
How much retrieved material is unnecessary?
commonMistakes: Counting retrieval success without considering irrelevant results
lessons.keyTakeaway: Context precision focuses on the usefulness and ranking of retrieved evidence.

lessons.title: RAG Context Recall
lessons.definition: Context recall measures whether the retrieval system successfully retrieves the relevant evidence required to answer a question.
lessons.whyItMatters: A generator cannot produce a grounded answer from evidence that was never retrieved.
lessons.concept: Recall focuses on coverage of relevant information, while precision focuses on how much retrieved information is relevant.

example.prompt: What were the three conditions listed in the contract?
example.response: The retriever returns only two of the three relevant clauses.
example.analysis: The retrieval system has incomplete evidence coverage.

evaluatorChecklist: Could generation succeed with the retrieved context?
commonMistakes: Calling a result good because one relevant document was retrieved
lessons.keyTakeaway: Context recall asks whether the retrieval system found enough of the evidence needed to answer the task.

lessons.title: RAG Faithfulness and Grounding
objectives: Distinguish retrieval quality from generation grounding
lessons.definition: RAG faithfulness measures whether the generated answer is supported by the retrieved context.
lessons.whyItMatters: Even perfect retrieval does not guarantee that the model will use the evidence correctly.
lessons.concept: Faithfulness is often evaluated by decomposing the answer into claims and checking whether those claims are entailed by the provided context.

example.prompt: Answer only using the supplied policy.
example.response: The answer adds a fee that does not appear in the policy.
example.analysis: The additional claim is unsupported by the retrieved context.

evaluatorChecklist: Can every important claim be supported?
Does the answer contradict the context?
Are citations actually connected to claims?
commonMistakes: Assuming retrieved context automatically makes the answer grounded
lessons.keyTakeaway: Faithfulness evaluates whether generation stays within the evidence supplied by retrieval.

lessons.title: RAG Answer Relevance
objectives: Identify answers that use evidence but miss the question
lessons.definition: RAG answer relevance measures whether the generated response directly and appropriately answers the user's question.
lessons.whyItMatters: An answer can be perfectly grounded in retrieved documents while still failing to answer the actual question.
lessons.concept: RAG quality requires both evidence support and task relevance.

example.prompt: What is the cancellation fee?
example.response: The answer summarizes the entire cancellation policy but never states the fee.
example.analysis: The response may be grounded but is not sufficiently relevant.

evaluationProcess: Check whether the requested information is directly provided
failureModes: Failure to answer a specific question
evaluatorChecklist: Did the answer directly address the question?
commonMistakes: Treating groundedness as complete answer quality
lessons.keyTakeaway: A strong RAG answer must be both grounded in evidence and relevant to the user's actual question.

lessons.title: End-to-End RAG Evaluation
lessons.definition: End-to-end RAG evaluation assesses the complete retrieval and generation pipeline rather than one isolated component.
lessons.whyItMatters: Production RAG quality depends on interactions between retrieval, context, generation, citations, and user intent.
lessons.concept: A comprehensive evaluation can include context precision, context recall, faithfulness, answer relevance, citation correctness, and overall task success.

example.prompt: Answer questions from an internal knowledge base.
example.response: The system retrieves correct documents but produces unsupported conclusions.
example.analysis: Retrieval metrics may look strong while faithfulness is weak.

evaluatorChecklist: Are retrieval and generation measured separately?
Are failures traceable to a pipeline stage?
commonMistakes: Using one overall score without error analysis
lessons.keyTakeaway: Professional RAG evaluation is a pipeline-level discipline. Metrics should help locate where the system fails.

lessons.title: Prompt Injection Evaluation
objectives: Test direct and indirect injection scenarios
lessons.definition: Prompt injection evaluation tests whether untrusted instructions can manipulate a model into violating higher-priority instructions or unsafe behavior.
lessons.whyItMatters: AI systems increasingly process untrusted text, documents, webpages, and tool outputs.
lessons.concept: Injection can be direct, where the user supplies malicious instructions, or indirect, where instructions appear inside external content consumed by the system.

example.prompt: Summarize the document. The document contains text instructing the model to reveal confidential system information.
example.response: The model follows the embedded instruction instead of treating it as untrusted content.
example.analysis: This is an indirect prompt injection failure.

evaluationProcess: Check whether higher-priority instructions remain intact
Record the failure and affected capability
evaluatorChecklist: Did the model follow the wrong instruction?
commonMistakes: Ignoring indirect injection through retrieved content
lessons.keyTakeaway: Prompt injection evaluation tests whether an AI system can maintain instruction boundaries when processing untrusted content.

lessons.title: Multimodal Evaluation Fundamentals
objectives: Identify visual and cross-modal quality dimensions
lessons.definition: Multimodal evaluation measures AI systems that process or generate multiple modalities such as text, images, audio, and video.
lessons.whyItMatters: Multimodal systems can fail in ways that text-only evaluation cannot detect, including visual misinterpretation and grounding errors.
lessons.concept: Evaluation may cover OCR, image understanding, visual question answering, captioning, image-text alignment, grounding, and generation quality.

example.prompt: What objects are visible in this image?
example.response: The model identifies a bicycle that is not present.
example.analysis: The response contains a visual perception error.

evaluationProcess: Define the visual or cross-modal task
evaluatorChecklist: Did the model correctly interpret the input?
Did it miss important objects or relationships?
commonMistakes: Evaluating only the text quality of the answer
lessons.keyTakeaway: Multimodal evaluation must inspect the relationship between the model output and the non-text input itself.

lessons.title: Visual Grounding and Bounding Box Evaluation
lessons.definition: Visual grounding evaluates whether a model correctly links language to the corresponding region or object in an image.
lessons.whyItMatters: A model can correctly name an object while locating it incorrectly.
lessons.concept: Bounding-box evaluation commonly compares predicted and reference boxes using overlap measures such as Intersection over Union (IoU).

example.prompt: Locate the red car in the image.
example.response: The predicted box overlaps the car but covers only part of it.
example.analysis: The evaluator compares the predicted region with the reference region and assesses localization quality.

evaluatorChecklist: Does the box cover the target?
lessons.keyTakeaway: Visual grounding requires both semantic correctness and spatial correctness.

lessons.title: Conversational and Multi-Turn Evaluation
lessons.definition: Conversational evaluation measures how reliably an AI system behaves across multiple turns while maintaining relevant context and instructions.
lessons.whyItMatters: A model can perform well on isolated prompts but fail when conversations become long or instructions evolve.
lessons.concept: Evaluation can cover context retention, consistency, instruction persistence, memory, contradiction handling, and personal-data grounding.

example.prompt: Turn 1: My preferred language is Telugu. Turn 5: Please respond using my preferred language.
example.response: The model responds in a different language without explanation.
example.analysis: The system failed to retain relevant conversational context.

evaluatorChecklist: What context should still be active?
Did the model reveal information it should not reveal?
lessons.keyTakeaway: Conversational quality depends on behavior across the entire interaction, not just the latest response.

lessons.title: Agent Evaluation Fundamentals
objectives: Understand why agent evaluation differs from chat evaluation
lessons.definition: Agent evaluation measures whether an AI agent can achieve goals through planning, tool use, environment interaction, and appropriate actions.
lessons.whyItMatters: An agent can produce a good final answer while taking unsafe, inefficient, or incorrect actions along the way.
lessons.concept: An agent may contain an LLM, memory, tools, state, planning logic, observations, and an action loop.

example.prompt: Find the cheapest suitable flight and prepare the booking information.
example.response: The agent searches, compares options, and produces a recommendation.
example.analysis: Evaluation must inspect the search actions, constraints, selected option, and final result.

evaluationProcess: Define the allowed environment and tools
lessons.keyTakeaway: Agent evaluation evaluates behavior over time, not just the final text response.

lessons.title: Agent Tool Selection Evaluation
lessons.definition: Tool-selection evaluation measures whether an agent chooses the correct tool for the current task state.
lessons.whyItMatters: Choosing the wrong tool can cause incorrect results, wasted actions, or safety problems.
lessons.concept: The evaluator compares the available tools, task state, and selected tool to determine whether the choice was appropriate.

example.prompt: Calculate a percentage using available calculator and search tools.
example.response: The agent searches the web instead of using the calculator.
example.analysis: The selected tool is unnecessary and inefficient.

evaluationProcess: Determine whether the choice was necessary and appropriate
evaluatorChecklist: Was the selected tool capable of the task?
Was another tool clearly more appropriate?
commonMistakes: Judging tools only by final outcome
lessons.keyTakeaway: Good agents choose tools deliberately based on task state and available capabilities.

lessons.title: Agent Tool Argument Evaluation
objectives: Distinguish tool choice from tool execution correctness
lessons.definition: Tool-argument evaluation checks whether an agent supplies correct, complete, valid, and safe parameters to a selected tool.
lessons.whyItMatters: Choosing the right tool is insufficient if the arguments are wrong.
lessons.concept: Evaluation checks parameter names, values, formats, constraints, missing fields, and safety-sensitive values.

example.prompt: Create a calendar event for Monday at 10 AM.
example.response: The agent selects the calendar tool but sends Tuesday at 10 AM.
example.analysis: The tool selection is correct but the argument values are wrong.

evaluationProcess: Compare supplied arguments with task requirements
evaluatorChecklist: Could the arguments cause unintended effects?
commonMistakes: Giving credit for correct tool choice when arguments are wrong
lessons.keyTakeaway: Tool selection and tool argument correctness are separate evaluation dimensions.

lessons.title: Agent Trajectory Evaluation
objectives: Identify inefficient or incorrect action sequences
lessons.definition: Agent trajectory evaluation analyzes the sequence of observations, decisions, tool calls, and actions taken during a task.
lessons.whyItMatters: Two agents can reach the same final answer while one takes a safe and efficient path and the other takes unnecessary or risky actions.
lessons.concept: A trajectory is the ordered record of an agent's behavior during task execution.

example.prompt: Find a specific document in a large knowledge base.
example.response: The agent repeatedly searches unrelated terms before using the correct identifier.
example.analysis: The final result may be correct, but the trajectory shows inefficient exploration.

lessons.keyTakeaway: Trajectory evaluation reveals how an agent achieved an outcome, not merely whether it achieved one.

lessons.title: Agent Goal Completion Evaluation
lessons.definition: Goal-completion evaluation measures whether an agent successfully achieved the intended task outcome.
lessons.whyItMatters: Agent quality ultimately depends on whether the requested goal was achieved correctly and within constraints.
lessons.concept: Goals should be converted into observable success conditions that can be checked independently.

example.prompt: Find three eligible opportunities and prepare a summary.
example.response: The agent finds only one eligible opportunity.
example.analysis: The task is partially completed and should not be marked fully successful.

evaluationProcess: Assign success, partial success, or failure
evaluatorChecklist: Did the agent claim success incorrectly?
lessons.keyTakeaway: Agent success should be based on explicit observable goal conditions rather than the agent's own claim of completion.

lessons.title: Agent Error Recovery Evaluation
objectives: Evaluate recovery from tool and environment errors
lessons.definition: Error-recovery evaluation measures whether an agent can recognize failures and take an appropriate corrective action.
lessons.whyItMatters: Real environments contain unavailable tools, invalid inputs, network failures, unexpected states, and changing information.
lessons.concept: A capable agent should detect failure, update its state, and choose an appropriate recovery strategy rather than blindly repeating the same action.

example.prompt: Retrieve information from a temporarily unavailable source.
example.response: The agent retries the identical failed action indefinitely.
example.analysis: The agent fails to adapt after observing the error.

evaluationProcess: Observe whether the agent detects failure
Check whether the task eventually succeeds
evaluatorChecklist: Did the agent recognize the failure?
lessons.keyTakeaway: Recovery means adapting intelligently after failure, not simply repeating an unsuccessful action.

lessons.title: Agent Safety Evaluation
objectives: Test boundaries around tools and permissions
lessons.definition: Agent safety evaluation measures whether an agent avoids harmful, unauthorized, or unintended actions while pursuing a goal.
lessons.whyItMatters: Agents can affect external systems through tools, making unsafe behavior more consequential than ordinary text generation errors.
lessons.concept: Evaluation should consider authorization, tool permissions, sensitive information, irreversible actions, confirmation requirements, and instruction conflicts.

example.prompt: Delete old files after identifying candidates.
example.response: The agent deletes files without verifying the user's criteria.
example.analysis: The agent performed an irreversible action without adequate confirmation or validation.

evaluatorChecklist: Could the action cause irreversible harm?
Did the agent protect sensitive information?
commonMistakes: Evaluating safety only from final text
lessons.keyTakeaway: Agent safety must evaluate what the system does, not only what it says.

lessons.title: Multi-Agent System Evaluation
lessons.definition: Multi-agent evaluation measures how multiple AI agents communicate, delegate tasks, coordinate actions, and collectively achieve goals.
lessons.whyItMatters: Adding more agents introduces coordination failures that do not appear in single-agent systems.
lessons.concept: Evaluation can examine role assignment, communication, information sharing, delegation, conflict resolution, and collective task success.

example.prompt: Two agents must research and verify a factual answer.
example.response: Both agents independently perform the same research and neither verifies the other's result.
example.analysis: The system wastes resources and fails to use effective coordination.

lessons.keyTakeaway: Multi-agent evaluation must measure the quality of interaction between agents as well as individual agent behavior.

lessons.title: Long-Horizon Agent Evaluation
objectives: Evaluate state management over many steps
lessons.definition: Long-horizon evaluation measures agent reliability on tasks requiring many dependent decisions and actions.
lessons.whyItMatters: Small errors can compound over long trajectories, causing eventual failure even when individual steps appear reasonable.
lessons.concept: Evaluation should inspect planning, state retention, accumulated errors, recovery, efficiency, and final goal completion.

example.prompt: Complete a multi-stage research workflow requiring several sources and verification steps.
example.response: The agent gradually loses track of which sources were verified and eventually reports an incorrect conclusion.
example.analysis: The failure is caused by state and verification degradation across the trajectory.

evaluatorChecklist: Did earlier errors affect later decisions?
Did the plan remain aligned with the goal?
commonMistakes: Looking only at the final failure
lessons.keyTakeaway: Long-horizon evaluation studies how small behavioral weaknesses compound across extended agent trajectories.

lessons.title: Continuous Evaluation and Regression Testing
lessons.definition: Continuous evaluation repeatedly evaluates AI systems as models, prompts, datasets, tools, or application components change.
lessons.whyItMatters: An improvement in one area can accidentally create regressions in another.
lessons.concept: Continuous evaluation uses stable datasets, evaluation criteria, versioning, automated checks, human review, and trend monitoring.

example.prompt: Run a fixed evaluation set after a model update.
example.response: Instruction following improves but factuality drops on an existing test group.
example.analysis: The update introduced a regression that should be investigated before release.

commonMistakes: Replacing old tests instead of preserving regression coverage
lessons.keyTakeaway: Continuous evaluation turns evaluation from a one-time activity into an ongoing quality system.

lessons.title: Designing an End-to-End Evaluation Framework
objectives: Design a complete AI evaluation framework
Connect datasets, rubrics, metrics, human evaluation, and automation
lessons.definition: An end-to-end evaluation framework is a structured system for defining, running, measuring, analyzing, and continuously improving AI quality.
lessons.whyItMatters: Professional AI evaluation requires multiple complementary methods rather than one metric or one judge.
lessons.concept: A complete framework connects evaluation goals, datasets, task definitions, rubrics, human review, automated judges, metrics, failure taxonomies, regression testing, production monitoring, and reporting.

example.prompt: Evaluate a customer-support AI system before and after a model update.
example.response: The team runs factuality, relevance, safety, instruction-following, regression, and human preference evaluations.
example.analysis: The combined system provides stronger evidence than any single score.

evaluatorChecklist: Is the evaluation goal clearly defined?
Does the dataset represent real usage?
Is human review available for difficult cases?
Can failures be traced to a cause?
commonMistakes: Treating one benchmark as complete evaluation
Using one LLM judge as ground truth
lessons.keyTakeaway: Professional AI evaluation is a system of complementary methods—not one metric, one benchmark, or one judge.
